Claude Monet. A French painter and founder of Impressionism born in eighteen forty, Monet revolutionized painting by prioritizing light, color, and optical sensation over precise detail. Based in rural Normandy and Paris, Monet became obsessed with painting the same subjects under different conditions of light and atmosphere, most famously the Rouen Cathedral, haystacks, and water lilies. His radical approach to depicting fleeting visual impressions transformed painting into a vehicle for capturing moments of perception rather than static forms.

Born in Paris but raised in Le Havre, where he discovered landscape painting and early Impressionist peers like Eugène Boudin. He pioneered the technique of series painting, returning obsessively to the same motif: haystacks, poplars, the Rouen Cathedral, capturing how light transforms their appearance across hours and seasons.

His painting Impression, Sunrise in eighteen seventy-two depicting the harbor at Le Havre at dawn was mocked by critics. The term "Impressionism" was born as mockery but became the movement's name. Later life beginning in eighteen eighty-three centered at Giverny, where he built an elaborate Japanese garden with a water lily pond that occupied him for the final three decades.

The water lilies series from the eighteen nineties through nineteen twenties grew increasingly abstract and immersive. These late works anticipated modernism and influenced abstract expressionists. He struggled with cataracts in old age, which altered his color perception and intensified the reds and oranges of his later paintings. Once a medical tragedy, this is now celebrated as visionary. He allied with other Impressionists but outlasted them, continuing to innovate until his death. Monet connects to Impressionism as the artistic movement he founded and exemplified, to the Seine River as the subject he painted obsessively, to the water lilies as the monumental series that consumed his final decades, to Paris as his birthplace and center of the Impressionist movement, to Pierre-Auguste Renoir as a fellow Impressionist pioneer, and to Japanese aesthetics as reflected in his Giverny garden and water lilies.
